Inside Mullin's Two Percent 

My old friend Willie had a saying for moments like this: I don't know how you did this, but I know you did this. He wasn't claiming to see the hands. He was refusing to pretend the result was an accident. What follows is that kind of inference. It's an abductive leap, and I'm calling it by its name. I don't have the forensics. I have the pattern, and I have the motive. 

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin went on Hannity Monday night and Squawk Box Tuesday morning and said, more than once, that he can say with 98% certainty the recent outages were not a cyberattack. I'll start there. If the question is whether a foreign hacker kicked in the door from outside, the Secretary has looked harder than I have, and he says no. But 98 is not 100, and a careful man doesn't leave 2% on the table by accident. He ruled out a footprint from outside. He did not rule out a hand from inside. That's the room I'm walking into. 

November 13. The FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop. L3Harris contractors were swapping copper for fiber at a remote radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, when a new Juniper router began flooding the FAA's network with roughly 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds. A second router, swapped in weeks earlier at a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, did the same thing. Of 22 en-route centers, 17 destabilized. The FAA shut off the broadcast function on about 60 similar routers as a precaution.

Listen to who's holding the bag. HPE, which owns Juniper, says the equipment did exactly what the installer's configuration told it to do. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says it was either contractor error or faulty equipment. Some aviation experts have said publicly that one router taking down that much of the system is hard to believe. And the FBI is involved out of an abundance of caution. Two routers, two sites, weeks apart, the same behavior. That's not a fluke. That's a configuration, and somebody configured it. The Amarillo swap weeks earlier reads as preparation, not detonation — the same way the Microsoft defect slept since July before it woke.

Now the inbox. On November 12 and 13, Outlook and Exchange Online went dark in more than 70 countries for more than 24 hours, one of the longest outages in Microsoft's history. Microsoft's own preliminary report traces it to a latent defect introduced in July, in a Windows fix written specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers. The bug detonated only under heavy load on newer, high-core-count servers. Microsoft's load testing ran on weaker hardware with fewer cores and a different traffic mix, so it never caught it. Then a routine Teams traffic reroute on November 11 pushed load onto the affected gateway. The bug woke up, the system cascaded, and restarted servers were slammed by waiting traffic and died again. Microsoft ruled out malicious activity, and it ruled out AI.

Read that slowly. A flaw sleeps since July, invisible to the company's own tests, and wakes only under one specific hardware profile and one specific traffic condition. Then the condition arrives. I'm not saying Microsoft is lying. I'm saying that's what it would look like. 

Then the money. On November 16, JPMorgan Chase confirmed a software bug in on-premises hardware systems and said it was not cyber related. Wells Fargo, Bank of America, U.S. Bank, Truist, Capital One and Zelle all felt it, but by Chase's own account only where they were party to a transaction with Chase. Chase was the single point of failure, and everyone else was downstream. Transactions were posting normally by about 6:30 p.m. Eastern...

-- Joseph Fosco 
November 17, 2026

Larry Magid, CEO of the Internet Safety Organization, Connect Safely:: “This recent NSA outage is on top of numerous other outages over the last week, starting with Microsoft Outlook, which disrupted email around the world, the FAA outage from Friday that grounded most flights in the US, a United Airlines outage, a number of banks that lost access to some online services, and even Apple's iCloud sign-in failures. ”
NSA Net is used for internally communicating classified and sensitive information. The report says there's no evidence that the issue stems from a cyber attack.
